plan.topic: Plague in US national parks and the Southwest: a prevention checklist for hikers, campers and pet owners (CDC)
plan.angle: Title: 'Plague in the US West: 5 CDC Prevention Tips for Hikers, Campers and Pet Owners'. Slide 1: 'An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the US (CDC, range 0–17; reviewed Oct 7, 2026).' Slide 2: where cases occur per CDC, plus human cases vs animal cases. Tips, each with the CDC page that says it: avoid sick or dead animals (contact your local health department about disposal); DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing; flea control for pets (add the cat-toxicity caveat only with a source); don't let free-roaming pets in endemic areas sleep on your bed; red flags after a trip, then contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention the trip. Calm fact in CDC's own wording about the 1924–25 Los Angeles epidemic. Short dated Irkutsk status line. Last slide: 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
plan.working_title: Plague in US National Parks: 6 CDC Prevention Tips for Hikers and Pet Owners
plan.why: An evergreen topic refreshed by the Oct 7 Outside and AP coverage. It is our best-performing format (plague plus place plus CDC number plus prevention) turned into a checklist people save, with a new angle on outdoor trips rather than case counts. | fact-check: Confirmed on CDC's statistics page (reviewed Oct 7, 2026): 'An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the United States', range 0–17, with cases mainly in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada. Problems: (1) CDC doesn't mention national parks, so the title has to say 'the rural West' or 'the Southwest'. (2) CDC's pets-in-bed tip is scoped: 'Do not allow dogs or cats that roam free in endemic areas to sleep on your bed.' Keep that scope. (3) The repellent tip should match CDC: DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing, and follow the label. (4) CDC's prevention page (reviewed Mar 5, 2025) doesn't show the cat-toxicity line or the prairie-dog line in what I checked. Find a CDC page that says them, or drop them. (5) For the 1924 fact, CDC's wording is 'The last urban plague epidemic in the United States occurred in Los Angeles from 1924 through 1925.' Quote that rather than 'no person-to-person spread since 1924' unless a CDC page states the latter. (6) The title says 6 tips but the angle lists 5. (7) Carousels have reached 0–2 accounts per the playbook, so consider making this a Short.

package.title: Plague in the US West: 5 CDC Prevention Tips for Hikers, Campers and Pet Owners

social.instagram_caption:
Planning a hike or camping trip out West? Plague still shows up in parts of the rural western US, and the CDC has a simple prevention checklist for hikers, campers and pet owners.

- About 5 human plague cases are reported each year in the US on average (CDC), and most of those cases occur in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada.
- People usually get it from an infected rodent flea bite or by handling an infected animal (CDC).
- CDC's tips: wear gloves around sick or dead animals, use insect repellent outdoors (follow the label), keep pets on flea control (never use dog flea products on cats), keep free-roaming pets off your bed in plague areas, and reduce rodent habitat around your home, work and campsite.
- After a trip to a plague area, watch for fever, a swollen painful lymph node, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain (not a full list, see CDC). If you notice any of these, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention the trip.

Save this for your next trip West, and send it to your camping buddy.
Have you ever seen a plague notice posted at a trailhead or campground?

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

#PlagueFacts #HikingSafety #CampingTips #PetSafety #PublicHealth #OutdoorSafety

factcheck.summary: I checked every claim against the live CDC and EPA pages on 2026-10-10. They're accurate, the quotes are word for word, and the review/update dates match the pages: CDC Maps and Statistics was reviewed Oct 7, 2026; Preventing Plague Mar 5, 2025; Signs and Symptoms May 15, 2024; About Plague Aug 24, 2026; the EPA page was updated Jun 10, 2026. Specifically: the "average of five" (range 0–17) wording matches exactly. Both regions match. The 1924–1925 Los Angeles quote is exact. The transmission routes, the gloves, DEET and permethrin advice, flea control, "see a vet", the free-roaming pets/bed rule and the dead-animals advice all match CDC. The symptoms for each form match CDC, and all 4 pneumonic signs are present. The EPA line about dog products on cats is real. The title is 81 characters and starts with "Plague". The CTA slide has the disclaimer, the "If you're worried, talk to a health professional" line and the urgent-contact line. The piece is calm and doesn't mention the Irkutsk case, so it doesn't need a dated Irkutsk status line and doesn't make any status claim. All five issues are minor wording fixes, with an exact replacement for each.

issues.location: Slide 5 (checklist), item 5, plus the title and the slide 5 headline
issues.claim: "5 CDC tips" with item 5 "Know the red flags"
issues.problem: CDC's Preventing Plague page lists 5 measures, and the first is "Reduce rodent habitat around your home, workplace, and recreational areas." The carousel drops that one and swaps in a symptoms item from a different page. So "5 CDC Prevention Tips" isn't quite CDC's list, and the main environmental tip is missing. Slide 6 already covers the red flags.
issues.fix: Replace item 5 with: {"label": "Reduce rodent habitat", "detail": "Around home, work and campsites (CDC)", "icon": "house"}. Keep slide 6 for the red flags. In the slide 5 body, change "Red flags: CDC Signs and Symptoms of Plague." to "Then see the red flags on the next slide."

issues.problem: This is broader than CDC, which says "if you are handling or skinning potentially infected animals."
issues.fix: Label: "Gloves for handling sick or dead animals"; detail: "Ask local health dept about safe disposal"

issues.claim: DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing; follow label
issues.problem: This is accurate, but on a slide aimed at pet owners it's missing a safety caveat: permethrin is highly toxic to cats. CDC also says DEET can go on clothing too.
issues.fix: Detail: "DEET on skin or clothing, permethrin on clothing only; follow label, keep permethrin away from cats"

issues.claim: Headache, chills, weakness: Common early signs
issues.problem: CDC doesn't call these "early signs". It lists them by form, and headache isn't listed for septicemic plague. The label is our inference, presented as CDC's.

issues.claim: Today's human cases cluster in the rural West (CDC)
issues.problem: CDC's wording is "typically occurred in the rural West". "Cluster" is slightly stronger than that.
issues.fix: Body: "CDC: 'The last urban plague epidemic in the United States occurred in Los Angeles from 1924 through 1925.' Since the mid-20th century, US plague has typically occurred in the rural West (CDC)."
